title: Mastering Korean Drinking Etiquette Rules: A Salaryman's Insider Guide
tldr: Korean drinking etiquette is fundamentally about showing respect and acknowledging hierarchy, especially during hoesik (company dinners).
Key actions include pouring and receiving drinks with two hands, and turning your head away from elders or superiors when drinking.
While these rules can seem complex, foreigners often receive leniency, but making a genuine effort to understand them is highly appreciated.

content:
📅 Updated 2026.11.02
Key takeaways
  • Korean drinking etiquette is fundamentally about showing respect and acknowledging hierarchy, especially during hoesik (company dinners).
  • Key actions include pouring and receiving drinks with two hands, and turning your head away from elders or superiors when drinking.
  • While these rules can seem complex, foreigners often receive leniency, but making a genuine effort to understand them is highly appreciated.
👤 This is for readers who want to understand not just what to do, but why Korean drinking etiquette rules exist, and how they play out in real life as of November 2026.

You've probably seen K-dramas or YouTube videos showing Koreans clinking glasses and turning away to drink. It looks a bit mysterious, right? You're wondering, "What's the big deal? Can't I just drink normally?" The short answer is: these are more than just quirky habits. They're deeply rooted in showing respect, acknowledging hierarchy, and fostering a unique sense of community, especially during hoesik (the after-work company dinner) or any social gathering with elders. As a salaryman in Seoul, navigating these rituals is just part of my weekly routine. Right now, in November 2026, while some things are loosening up, the core rules of Korean drinking etiquette rules are still very much alive.

The Bow, The Pour, The Receive: Understanding the Core Basics

The fundamental rule of Korean drinking etiquette is to show respect, primarily through your hands and body language. When someone older or higher in rank pours you a drink, you should always receive the glass with two hands. This isn't just a polite gesture; it's a visual cue of deference. You don't just grab it. Similarly, when you pour for an elder, you also use two hands – one supporting the bottom of the bottle or glass, the other on the neck. It's like a mini-bow with your hands. Once you've received your drink, if you're drinking in front of an elder or superior, you must turn your head and body slightly away from them to take your sip. This specific action, which always makes foreigners curious, is about not letting the elder see you consume alcohol directly, a further sign of respect. At my very first hoesik, I watched my sunbae (senior colleague) like a hawk, trying to mimic every move. I fumbled the two-hand pour, and he just chuckled, but I knew I had to get it right.

Point: Your hands and posture speak volumes about your respect here.

The Shot Glass, The Cheers, The Refill: Keeping the Flow Going

Never let an elder's glass be empty, and never, ever pour your own drink – these are the golden rules for maintaining the flow of a Korean drinking session. Once a round of soju (Korean distilled spirit) or beer begins, it's an unspoken duty to make sure everyone's glass is full, especially those above you in age or status. You'll see someone constantly scanning the table. If a glass is empty, you jump in and pour. And when it's your turn, someone will pour for you. This creates a continuous cycle of interaction and care, reinforcing the group dynamic. We often do konbae (cheers) before taking our first shot, shouting it out with enthusiasm. Honestly, after a few rounds, the pressure to refill everyone's glass can feel a bit like a full-time job, especially if the boss is a fast drinker. I've definitely learned to pace myself, sometimes subtly pouring less for myself if I need a break.

Point: It's about collective participation, not individual drinking.

Beyond the Table: The Unwritten Rules of the Hoesik Journey

Korean drinking etiquette extends far beyond just the actual act of drinking; it encompasses the entire hoesik (company dinner) experience, which is a key part of team bonding. A hoesik isn't just one round of food and drinks; it's often a multi-stage event. After the first restaurant (il-cha), you might move to a second spot for more drinks (i-cha), often a hof (beer pub) or a noraebang (karaoke room) for singing. The expectation is that you participate in all rounds, or at least show good reason if you need to leave early. Leaving before the most senior person is generally a no-go unless you have a truly unavoidable excuse. I've been to hoesiks that started at 6 PM and didn't wrap up until well past midnight, with everyone moving from grilled pork belly to a crowded pub, then to a private karaoke room. It's exhausting sometimes, but it’s where a lot of workplace relationships are built. Even at the noraebang, you're expected to cheer on your coworkers, no matter how bad their singing is.

Point: Hoesik is a marathon, not a sprint, and participation is key.

The “Can I Refuse?” Question: Navigating Peer Pressure and Exceptions

While showing respect often means accepting drinks, it is absolutely possible to politely refuse alcohol in Korea, though the method and timing are crucial. You can't just blurt out "No thanks!" There's a certain nunchi (the art of reading the room) involved. A common tactic is to say, "Jeoneun oneul momi jom an joaseo" (저는 오늘 몸이 좀 안 좋아서 - My body isn't feeling so good today), or "Naeil achim-e jungyohan ireumi isseoseo" (내일 아침에 중요한 일 - I have something important tomorrow morning). Sometimes, just accepting the drink and taking very small, slow sips throughout the round is enough. The culture is slowly changing, especially among younger Koreans, and there's more understanding if you genuinely don't want to drink. In my office, I've seen younger colleagues subtly turn their glass upside down or just keep it full, indicating they're not drinking more. It’s a delicate balance; you want to be polite, but not feel forced.

Point: Refusal is possible, but requires tact and a little acting.

A Foreigner's Advantage: When the Rules Bend (and why)

Here's the good news: as a foreigner, you're often given a significant amount of leeway when it comes to Korean drinking etiquette rules. Koreans understand that these customs aren't universal, and they generally appreciate the effort you make more than the flawless execution. Small mistakes – like forgetting to turn away or accidentally pouring your own drink – will usually be met with a kind smile or a gentle correction, rather than judgment. The first time a foreign coworker tried to pour soju with two hands, everyone at our table genuinely seemed pleased. It shows you're paying attention and you care about fitting in, even a little bit. Don't let the complexity deter you; just showing a willingness to learn goes a long way. This isn't about perfectly mimicking every move; it's about signaling respect and openness to the culture.

Point: Effort trumps perfection, and goodwill is your biggest asset.

Walk through it with me

  1. 1
    Receive Your Drink with Respect
    When an elder or superior offers you a drink, always accept the glass with two hands as a sign of deference.
  2. 2
    Pour for Others Thoughtfully
    Never pour your own drink; instead, actively look to refill others' glasses, especially elders, using two hands on the bottle.
  3. 3
    Turn Away to Take Your Sip
    When drinking in front of someone older or higher in rank, subtly turn your head and body away from them to take your sip.
  4. 4
    Participate in Cheers (Konbae)
    Join in with enthusiasm during group cheers, often shouting 'konbae!' before taking a shot or sip.
  5. 5
    Accept Refills Gracefully
    While you can pace yourself with small sips, it's generally polite to accept refills when offered, especially early in the gathering.

Frequently asked questions

Q. Is it okay to refuse a drink in Korea?

A. Yes, you can refuse, but do so politely and strategically, perhaps citing an early morning commitment or not feeling well, rather than a blunt 'no'.

Q. Why do Koreans turn away when drinking alcohol?

A. Turning away from elders or superiors while drinking is a traditional gesture of respect, preventing them from directly seeing you consume alcohol.

Q. Should I pour my own drink at a Korean dinner?

A. No, it's considered impolite to pour your own drink; wait for someone else to pour for you, and in turn, you should pour for others, especially elders.

Q. What does 'hoesik' mean and how does it relate to drinking?

A. Hoesik (회식) is a company dinner or outing, often involving multiple rounds of food and drinks, where team bonding and hierarchy are reinforced through specific drinking etiquette.

Q. Do these rules apply to casual drinking with friends?

A. While the strictness lessens significantly among close friends of similar age, the underlying principles of respect still apply if there's an age gap, but it's much more relaxed.

한국 음주 예절 규칙 마스터하기: 샐러리맨의 내부자 가이드

여러분은 한국인들이 잔을 부딪치고 몸을 돌려 술을 마시는 K-드라마나 유튜브 영상을 본 적이 있을 것입니다. 좀 신비롭게 보이죠? 여러분은 "뭐가 그렇게 대단해? 그냥 평범하게 마시면 안 돼?"라고 생각할 것입니다. 짧게 답하자면: 이것들은 단순한 기이한 습관 이상입니다. 그것들은 존경을 표하고, 위계를 인정하며, 독특한 공동체 의식을 함양하는 데 깊이 뿌리박고 있습니다. 특히 회식(퇴근 후 회사 저녁 식사)이나 어른들과의 어떤 사교 모임에서 말이죠. 서울의 샐러리맨으로서 이러한 의식을 헤쳐나가는 것은 제 주간 일상의 일부입니다. 지금, 2026년 11월에, 일부 규칙들이 느슨해지고 있지만, 한국 음주 예절의 핵심 규칙들은 여전히 매우 살아있습니다.

## 절하기, 따르기, 받기: 핵심 기본 이해하기

**한국 음주 예절의 근본적인 규칙은 주로 손과 몸짓을 통해 존경을 표하는 것입니다.** 나이가 많거나 직급이 높은 사람이 술을 따라줄 때, 항상 두 손으로 잔을 받아야 합니다. 이것은 단순한 공손한 제스처가 아닙니다. 그것은 존경을 시각적으로 보여주는 신호입니다. 그냥 잡는 것이 아닙니다. 마찬가지로, 어른에게 술을 따를 때도 두 손을 사용합니다 – 한 손은 병이나 잔의 바닥을 받치고, 다른 한 손은 목을 잡습니다. 마치 손으로 하는 작은 절과 같습니다. 술을 받은 후, 어른이나 상사 앞에서 마실 때는, 그들에게서 머리와 몸을 약간 돌려 한 모금 마셔야 합니다. 외국인들을 항상 궁금하게 만드는 이 특정 행동은 어른이 여러분이 직접 술을 마시는 것을 보지 않게 하는 것으로, 또 다른 존경의 표시입니다. 제 첫 회식에서 저는 선배(선임 동료)를 매처럼 지켜보며 모든 동작을 따라 하려고 했습니다. 두 손으로 따르는 것을 서툴게 하자 그는 그저 껄껄 웃었지만, 저는 제대로 해야 한다는 것을 알았습니다.

> 요점: 여러분의 손과 자세는 여기서 여러분의 존경심에 대해 많은 것을 말해줍니다.

## 소주잔, 건배, 리필: 흐름 유지하기

**어른의 잔이 비어있게 두지 말고, 절대로, 절대로 자신의 잔에 술을 따르지 마세요 – 이것들은 한국 음주 자리의 흐름을 유지하기 위한 황금률입니다.** 소주(한국 증류주)나 맥주 한 잔이 시작되면, 특히 나이나 지위가 높은 사람들의 잔을 포함하여 모든 사람의 잔이 가득 차 있는지 확인하는 것은 암묵적인 의무입니다. 누군가가 끊임없이 테이블을 스캔하는 것을 볼 것입니다. 잔이 비어 있으면, 여러분이 나서서 따릅니다. 그리고 여러분 차례가 되면, 누군가가 여러분에게 따라줄 것입니다. 이것은 상호작용과 보살핌의 지속적인 순환을 만들어 그룹 역학을 강화합니다. 우리는 종종 첫 잔을 마시기 전에 *건배*를 외치며 열정적으로 소리칩니다. 솔직히, 몇 잔 돌고 나면, 모든 사람의 잔을 리필해야 한다는 압박감이 마치 풀타임 직업처럼 느껴질 수 있습니다. 특히 사장님이 술을 빨리 마시는 분이라면요. 저는 확실히 속도를 조절하는 법을 배웠고, 때로는 휴식이 필요하면 제 잔에 미묘하게 적게 따르기도 합니다.

> 요점: 이것은 개인적인 음주가 아니라 집단적인 참여에 관한 것입니다.

## 테이블 너머: 회식 여정의 불문율

**한국 음주 예절은 단순히 술을 마시는 행위를 훨씬 넘어섭니다. 그것은 팀 유대의 핵심 부분인 전체 회식 경험을 포함합니다.** 회식은 한 번의 음식과 술로 끝나는 것이 아닙니다. 종종 여러 단계로 진행되는 행사입니다. 첫 번째 식당(일차) 후, 더 많은 술을 마시러 두 번째 장소(이차)로 이동할 수 있으며, 종종 *호프*(맥주 펍)나 노래를 부르기 위한 *노래방*(가라오케 룸)으로 갑니다. 모든 라운드에 참여하거나, 일찍 떠나야 할 경우 합당한 이유를 제시해야 합니다. 가장 높은 사람보다 먼저 떠나는 것은 일반적으로 피할 수 없는 변명이 없는 한 안 됩니다. 저는 오후 6시에 시작하여 자정 훨씬 넘어서야 끝난 회식에 가본 적이 있습니다. 모두가 삼겹살에서 붐비는 펍으로, 그리고 개인 노래방으로 이동했습니다. 때로는 피곤하지만, 많은 직장 관계가 형성되는 곳입니다. 노래방에서도 동료들의 노래 실력이 아무리 나빠도 응원해야 합니다.

> 요점: 회식은 단거리 경주가 아니라 마라톤이며, 참여가 핵심입니다.

## "거절할 수 있나요?" 질문: 동료 압력과 예외 다루기

**존경을 표하는 것이 종종 술을 받아들이는 것을 의미하지만, 한국에서 술을 정중하게 거절하는 것은 절대적으로 가능합니다. 단, 방법과 타이밍이 중요합니다.** "아니요, 괜찮습니다!"라고 그냥 툭 내뱉을 수는 없습니다. 어느 정도 눈치(상황을 읽는 기술)가 필요합니다. 흔한 전략은 "*저는 오늘 몸이 좀 안 좋아서*"라고 말하거나, "*내일 아침에 중요한 일이 있어서*"라고 말하는 것입니다. 때로는 술을 받고 라운드 내내 아주 작고 천천히 마시는 것만으로도 충분합니다. 문화는 서서히 변하고 있으며, 특히 젊은 한국인들 사이에서는 진정으로 술을 마시고 싶지 않을 때 더 많은 이해를 보여줍니다. 제 사무실에서는 젊은 동료들이 미묘하게 잔을 뒤집거나 그냥 가득 채워두어 더 이상 마시지 않겠다는 것을 나타내는 것을 보았습니다. 이것은 섬세한 균형입니다. 예의를 지키고 싶지만, 강요당하는 느낌을 받고 싶지는 않습니다.

> 요점: 거절은 가능하지만, 재치와 약간의 연기가 필요합니다.

## 외국인의 이점: 규칙이 유연해질 때 (그리고 그 이유)

**여기 좋은 소식이 있습니다: 외국인으로서 여러분은 한국 음주 예절 규칙에 관해서 상당한 재량권을 부여받는 경우가 많습니다.** 한국인들은 이러한 관습이 보편적이지 않다는 것을 이해하며, 일반적으로 완벽한 실행보다는 여러분이 기울이는 노력을 더 높이 평가합니다. 작은 실수 – 예를 들어 몸을 돌리는 것을 잊거나 실수로 자신의 잔에 술을 따르는 것 –은 보통 판단보다는 친절한 미소나 부드러운 교정으로 받아들여질 것입니다. 외국인 동료가 처음으로 두 손으로 소주를 따르려고 했을 때, 우리 테이블의 모든 사람들이 진심으로 기뻐하는 것 같았습니다. 그것은 여러분이 주의를 기울이고 있고, 조금이라도 어울리려고 노력한다는 것을 보여줍니다. 복잡함에 낙담하지 마세요. 배우려는 의지를 보여주는 것만으로도 큰 도움이 됩니다. 이것은 모든 동작을 완벽하게 모방하는 것이 아니라, 존경심과 문화에 대한 개방성을 나타내는 것입니다.

> 요점: 노력은 완벽함보다 중요하며, 선의가 가장 큰 자산입니다.

## Beyond the Table: The Unwritten Rules of the Hoesik Journey

Korean drinking etiquette extends far beyond just the actual act of drinking; it encompasses the entire hoesik (company dinner) experience, which is a key part of team bonding. A hoesik isn't just one round of food and drinks; it's often a multi-stage event. After the first restaurant (il-cha), you might move to a second spot for more drinks (i-cha), often a hof (beer pub) or a noraebang (karaoke room) for singing. The expectation is that you participate in all rounds, or at least show good reason if you need to leave early. Leaving before the most senior person is generally a no-go unless you have a truly unavoidable excuse. I've been to hoesiks that started at 6 PM and didn't wrap up until well past midnight, with everyone moving from grilled pork belly to a crowded pub, then to a private karaoke room. It's exhausting sometimes, but it’s where a lot of workplace relationships are built. Even at the noraebang, you're expected to cheer on your coworkers, no matter how bad their singing is.

> Point: Hoesik is a marathon, not a sprint, and participation is key.

## The “Can I Refuse?” Question: Navigating Peer Pressure and Exceptions

While showing respect often means accepting drinks, it is absolutely possible to politely refuse alcohol in Korea, though the method and timing are crucial. You can't just blurt out "No thanks!" There's a certain nunchi (the art of reading the room) involved. A common tactic is to say, "Jeoneun oneul momi jom an joaseo" (저는 오늘 몸이 좀 안 좋아서 - My body isn't feeling so good today), or "Naeil achim-e jungyohan ireumi isseoseo" (내일 아침에 중요한 일 - I have something important tomorrow morning). Sometimes, just accepting the drink and taking very small, slow sips throughout the round is enough. The culture is slowly changing, especially among younger Koreans, and there's more understanding if you genuinely don't want to drink. In my office, I've seen younger colleagues subtly turn their glass upside down or just keep it full, indicating they're not drinking more. It’s a delicate balance; you want to be polite, but not feel forced.

> Point: Refusal is possible, but requires tact and a little acting.

## A Foreigner's Advantage: When the Rules Bend (and why)

Here's the good news: as a foreigner, you're often given a significant amount of leeway when it comes to Korean drinking etiquette rules. Koreans understand that these customs aren't universal, and they generally appreciate the effort you make more than the flawless execution. Small mistakes – like forgetting to turn away or accidentally pouring your own drink – will usually be met with a kind smile or a gentle correction, rather than judgment. The first time a foreign coworker tried to pour soju with two hands, everyone at our table genuinely seemed pleased. It shows you're paying attention and you care about fitting in, even a little bit. Don't let the complexity deter you; just showing a willingness to learn goes a long way. This isn't about perfectly mimicking every move; it's about signaling respect and openness to the culture.

> Point: Effort trumps perfection, and goodwill is your biggest asset.

mainEntity.name: Is it okay to refuse a drink in Korea?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, you can refuse, but do so politely and strategically, perhaps citing an early morning commitment or not feeling well, rather than a blunt 'no'.

mainEntity.name: Why do Koreans turn away when drinking alcohol?

acceptedAnswer.text: Turning away from elders or superiors while drinking is a traditional gesture of respect, preventing them from directly seeing you consume alcohol.

mainEntity.name: Should I pour my own drink at a Korean dinner?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, it's considered impolite to pour your own drink; wait for someone else to pour for you, and in turn, you should pour for others, especially elders.

mainEntity.name: What does 'hoesik' mean and how does it relate to drinking?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hoesik (회식) is a company dinner or outing, often involving multiple rounds of food and drinks, where team bonding and hierarchy are reinforced through specific drinking etiquette.

mainEntity.name: Do these rules apply to casual drinking with friends?

acceptedAnswer.text: While the strictness lessens significantly among close friends of similar age, the underlying principles of respect still apply if there's an age gap, but it's much more relaxed.

step.name: Receive Your Drink with Respect
step.text: When an elder or superior offers you a drink, always accept the glass with two hands as a sign of deference.

step.name: Pour for Others Thoughtfully
step.text: Never pour your own drink; instead, actively look to refill others' glasses, especially elders, using two hands on the bottle.

step.name: Turn Away to Take Your Sip
step.text: When drinking in front of someone older or higher in rank, subtly turn your head and body away from them to take your sip.

step.name: Participate in Cheers (Konbae)
step.text: Join in with enthusiasm during group cheers, often shouting 'konbae!' before taking a shot or sip.

step.name: Accept Refills Gracefully
step.text: While you can pace yourself with small sips, it's generally polite to accept refills when offered, especially early in the gathering.
